summary: Describes requirements for roaming among dial-up Internet providers, meaning the ability to use several ISPs while keeping a formal relationship with only one. It lists criteria for judging roaming protocols. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine one phone plan that works in many towns. This lists what a system needs so your dial-up internet works with many companies.

questions: what are the criteria for roaming protocols
what does a roaming protocol need to do
how do isps authenticate roaming users
subtitle: What roaming protocols must do to work across multiple ISPs

tldr.problem: Before broadband was ubiquitous, dial-up users wanted to maintain a relationship with one ISP but roam to access points of other ISPs in a roaming consortium. Each consortium member needed different protocols for phone-book updates, authentication, and accounting—but there were no standards.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies requirements for roaming protocols in three areas: the phone book subsystem (finding access points), the authentication subsystem (proving identity and authorizing access), and the accounting subsystem (tracking resource use). The criteria use RFC 2119 language to distinguish must-haves from nice-to-haves.
tldr.outcome: The criteria became a benchmark for evaluating roaming protocols like RADIUS and EAP-based solutions. Later work, including the IETF's roaming protocols, used these requirements.

facts.label: Key requirement areas
facts.value: 6 (portability, security, scalability, RADIUS support, address assignment, accounting)

today: RFC 2477 is Informational and remains a useful reference for understanding roaming architecture, though dial-up roaming itself is obsolete. The principles—standardized identity formats, distributed authentication, and usage accounting—remain relevant to modern mobility management and federation systems.

sections.title: Roaming and Its Architecture
sections.content:
Roaming capability is the ability to use multiple Internet Service Providers (ISPs) while maintaining a formal customer relationship with only one. Before broadband, this was critical: a business traveler or a regional ISP needed worldwide dial-up access through a roaming consortium—a partnership of regional and national providers.

The roaming architecture has three subsystems. The phone book subsystem maintains and distributes a database of dial-in numbers, so users can find Points of Presence (POPs) wherever they are. The authentication subsystem verifies that a user is authorized to access a POP and configures the access session. The accounting subsystem tracks how many minutes, bytes, or other resources each user consumed, so the home ISP can bill them.

This document does not propose a single protocol. Instead, it specifies requirements that any roaming protocol or family of protocols must meet. These requirements cover portability, security, scalability, RADIUS integration, and more.
sections.plainLanguage: When you travel and use a local ISP's dial-up, your home ISP still bills you. For that to work, the two ISPs must exchange information about who you are, what you used, and how much to charge. This explains what they need to exchange.

sections.title: Phone Book and Discovery
sections.content:
The phone book subsystem has four functions: phone number presentation (showing users available numbers), phone number exchange (ISPs sharing updates with partners), phone book compilation (combining partners' data), and phone book update (sending new phone books to clients).

The RFC specifies that phone number presentation and exchange do not need standardization—vendors can implement them differently. But phone book update (delivering new phone books to client software) must be standardized, because users run client software on many devices and operating systems.

The phone book format must support attributes for phone numbers (like connection speed or access technology), service providers (coverage area, cost), and service configuration (proxy settings, VPN parameters). It must be extensible (new attributes can be added without breaking old clients), compact (to minimize download bandwidth), and support multiple languages and character sets.
sections.plainLanguage: Your laptop needs a list of phone numbers to dial. Different companies maintain that list. The challenge is keeping everyone's lists in sync, in a compact format, without requiring custom software for each ISP.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
When a user dials in, the receiving ISP (the local provider) must verify the user's identity and get authorization from the user's home ISP. The authentication subsystem covers five areas.

Connection management uses PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol), the standard protocol for dial-up. Identification requires a standardized format for the user ID and realm, so the local ISP can route the request to the home ISP. Verification of identity must support CHAP (Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol) and should support EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol); PAP should be avoided for security reasons. The system must be scalable to thousands of ISP members.

NAS configuration means the home ISP's authorization server sends configuration parameters to the local ISP's Network Access Server (NAS), so the user gets the right IP address, routing, and firewall rules. Address assignment can be dynamic or static, and must not preclude layer-2 tunneling (for VPNs) or Mobile IP. Security must include hop-by-hop integrity and confidentiality (for each link) and end-to-end attribute-level protection (so proxies can edit some fields but not tamper with critical ones).
sections.plainLanguage: When you call a roaming access point, it checks your password (or token) with your home ISP. Your home ISP tells the local ISP what IP address to give you and what rules apply. This must be secure, scalable, and work with existing systems like RADIUS.

sections.title: Accounting and Record Keeping
sections.content:
After a session ends, the local ISP reports usage to the user's home ISP so they can bill correctly. The accounting subsystem must provide real-time accounting, where usage is reported during and after a session (essential for fraud detection). It must define a standardized accounting record format that is compact and includes metrics like session duration, connection speed, port type, bytes sent and received, and disconnection reason.

The record format must be extensible, so new metrics (like QoS information or latency) can be added without breaking old systems. It must support both standard metrics and vendor-specific metrics, since ISPs may want to track proprietary information.
sections.plainLanguage: When your session ends, the local ISP needs to tell your home ISP how long you were connected, how much data you used, and why you disconnected. This data has to be standardized, encrypted, and reliably delivered so billing is accurate.

sections.title: Security and Compliance
sections.content:
A roaming protocol must include a thorough security analysis documenting threats and countermeasures, including fraud prevention and detection mechanisms. Hop-by-hop security protects traffic between each pair of systems (client to local ISP, local ISP to home ISP); this can be done with IPsec or other methods. End-to-end security ensures attribute-by-attribute integrity and confidentiality, so that data object security is possible even as packets pass through proxies that may edit them.

The RFC also establishes compliance language. A protocol is unconditionally compliant if it meets all must, must-not, should, and should-not requirements for its capabilities. A protocol is conditionally compliant if it meets the must and must-not requirements but not all should/should-not requirements. A protocol that violates a must or must-not requirement for a capability it claims to support is not compliant.
sections.plainLanguage: Roaming systems handle passwords, billing info, and personal usage data—all sensitive. The protocol must protect this data at every step and define a clear standard for when a protocol is good enough versus when it has security problems.
